vignette: Mark, a 36-year-old tax consultant from North America, married and of North American ethnicity, carries the weight of his military service with him daily. His journey into PTSD began six years ago when he was serving in Afghanistan. During a routine patrol, an improvised explosive device (IED) detonated near their convoy, leaving several comrades injured and Mark himself with shrapnel wounds that have since healed physically but left deep emotional scars. Mark's life as a tax consultant is methodical, precise, and predictable-qualities that he clings to for stability. However, the echoes of his combat experiences often disrupt this sense of control. He describes waking up in the middle of the night with intense sweating and heart palpitations, replaying the moment when the IED exploded over and over again. In these dreams, Mark relives the chaos and the sounds of shrapnel tearing through metal and flesh, his ears ringing with the deafening blast. At work, he finds solace in numbers and data-something tangible that doesn't change its form or meaning. However, even here, he struggles to focus when sudden loud noises, like a door slamming or a fire alarm going off, trigger an immediate fight-or-flight response. He feels his heart race and muscles tense as if he's back in combat mode, ready for danger at any moment. Mark tries to stay busy, often working late hours to avoid the silence of home where memories can flood him. His wife, Sarah, notices his distant behavior and growing irritability. Even though they share a comfortable life together, Mark finds himself on edge around her, feeling guilty that he cannot open up about what truly haunts him. He worries that his constant state of alertness is affecting their relationship; he's become short-tempered and overly critical, even with Sarah. On weekends, Mark used to enjoy hiking and camping with Sarah and friends, but now the thought of venturing into nature terrains brings back flashbacks of the rugged Afghan landscape. The sounds of leaves rustling or an unexpected loud noise can send him spiraling into a panic attack. Consequently, he avoids outdoor activities altogether, retreating instead to indoor hobbies like reading books on military history-a way to confront his fears indirectly. At times, Mark isolates himself from social gatherings, fearing that the crowded spaces might trigger another episode of hyperarousal or hypervigilance. The constant fear that something bad is about to happen has made him wary and suspicious of others' intentions, even those he trusts. His wife often comments on his lack of trust in her reassurances, which makes him feel like a burden. Despite these challenges, Mark continues to maintain his professional life with precision and competence. He excels at his work, finding comfort in the structured nature of tax law and regulations, where clear rules and procedures provide a semblance of order. However, this very compartmentalization is also part of his coping mechanism-keeping his traumatic experiences confined to specific mental compartments that he hopes will not spill into other aspects of his life. Recently, Mark has started noticing how the trauma affects his interactions with Sarah's extended family during holiday gatherings. The chaos and unpredictability of such settings often send him into a state of anxiety. He feels like everyone is watching him, waiting for him to break down or make a mistake. These episodes have led to several confrontations where he lashes out at minor inconveniences, leaving Sarah feeling bewildered about his behavior. As Mark navigates these challenges, he remains deeply aware that something significant needs to change. The constant tension and fear are taking their toll on both him and his relationship with Sarah. However, the idea of seeking help feels daunting; he worries it might reveal a part of himself he's not ready to confront openly. For now, Mark continues to find solace in the familiar routine of work and the quiet solitude of home, hoping that over time, things will slowly get better on their own. Through his daily life as a tax consultant, Mark grapples with the aftermath of his military service, trying to rebuild a semblance of normalcy amidst persistent reminders of his trauma.
